statement: To avoid a full mesh of TCP connections between WebSocket servers, put a Pub/Sub in the middle: every WebSocket server creates a single connection to it instead of one connection to every other server.
case_study: Inter-server delivery of Slack channel messages across WebSocket servers.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: A way to make it better is to not have these many TCP connections here, but instead put a Pub/Sub.

statement: The Pub/Sub used between WebSocket servers must be a real-time Pub/Sub such as Redis, not Kafka; Kafka would slow it down.
case_study: Slack real-time messaging design (the lecture's running case study).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It's a real-time Pub/Sub, not Kafka. Kafka would slow it down. It's a real-time Pub/Sub like Redis.

statement: With the Pub/Sub, the inter-server TCP connection overhead per WebSocket server drops to just one: in the example a server holds four user connections (A, B, C, D) plus one connection to the real-time Pub/Sub.
case_study: Slack real-time messaging design (the lecture's running case study).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So now your TCP connection overhead for inter-server communication is reduced to just one.

statement: A real-time Pub/Sub sends a message to everyone who is subscribed to it right now.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: send this message to everyone who is subscribed to it right now.

statement: A real-time Pub/Sub gives zero persistence: it does not store the message at the moment it relays it, unlike Kafka; it just pushes it to the subscribers.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It gives you zero persistence, zero

statement: Message flow with the Pub/Sub: when user A sends a message to Slack channel 1, its WebSocket server checks which of its own users are in channel 1 (B, C, D) and delivers to them, then sends the message to the real-time Pub/Sub, which pushes it to everyone subscribed.
case_study: Slack real-time messaging design (the lecture's running case study).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: it would check Slack channel one, BCD is connected, so BCD gets a message, and then it sends message to this real-time Pub/Sub.

statement: With a real-time Pub/Sub, a server that is not connected at the moment a message is published does not receive that message (the message goes to WS2, WS3, WS4 right there and then).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: In case a server wasn't connected, it would not receive this message.

statement: A real-time Pub/Sub does not guarantee delivery; its only guarantee is to send the message to everyone connected to it at that moment.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It does not guarantee delivery. What it guarantees is people who are connected at this moment to me, I'll just send a message...

statement: Redis is a great example of a real-time Pub/Sub tool.

verbatim: So this is real-time Pub/Sub, and one great example, what tool that is great example for that is Redis.

statement: The student then suggested that the routing service could cache the users' data.

speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: users data which is still slow, still slow, making a network call every time to get it where to send it, very slow, never.

statement: Adding a service for its own sake, just to tell where to forward a message, is overkill; the edge server can store that information.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Just adding a service for the sake of it, just to tell you where to forward it to is an over.

statement: In this system persistence of a sent message is guaranteed but the real-time notification is not (the message may get lost in Redis; the user sees it on refresh); for an enterprise application, guaranteed persistence is the more important part.
case_study: Slack real-time messaging design (the lecture's running case study).
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: So the notification part is not guaranteed there, but the persistence is guaranteed.

statement: With lots of users across many organizations, the inter-server Pub/Sub is not one Redis instance but a cluster of Redis.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: this is not just one Redis instance. These are multiple Redis, a cluster of Redis, right?

statement: The Balancer always returns the same edge server IP to all users of one organization, so everyone in that organization connects to one edge server; this minimizes IO on Redis, which then only carries the worst-case scenario traffic.
case_study: Slack real-time messaging design (the lecture's running case study).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: And everyone of that one organization connects to that one edge server.

statement: A public edge server can be attacked; putting it behind a load balancer adds one more hop, about five milliseconds of extra latency. If that latency is acceptable use the load balancer; if not, keep it public. Both are fine.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So five, five milliseconds of extended latency.

statement: Keeping edge servers public is fine because there is nothing sensitive on them: a route from the Balancer service that hands out IP addresses, a bunch of TCP connections, and one Kafka connection string that holds no secret and only pushes messages.
detail: Either keep it public on the internet with minimal critical things on it, or put it behind a load balancer and take the 3-5 ms extra hop.
case_study: Slack real-time messaging design (the lecture's running case study).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: And that's fine because there is no sensitive information here.

statement: A student suggested concluding that Redis Pub/Sub and Kafka are kind of the same.
detail: Teacher's correction: no - they differ in persistence and real-time behaviour (see the push/pull and persistence comparisons).
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: can we conclude that Redis Pub/Sub and Kafka kind of same?

statement: A student summarized the difference as 'Kafka is asynchronous, that's it'.
detail: Teacher's correction: he did not accept the synchronous/asynchronous framing; the difference is that Kafka is pull-based with persisted history while Redis Pub/Sub pushes with zero persistence.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: So, so the, and Kafka is asynchronous. That's it. Right.

statement: Kafka is pull-based (consumers pull messages from Kafka), while Redis Pub/Sub pushes messages to everyone connected.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Kafka is a pull-based thing. People, consumers pull message from Kafka. Redis Pub/Sub pushes message.

statement: Kafka gives persistence of historical messages; Redis gives zero persistence on Pub/Sub.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Kafka gives a persistence of historical messages. Redis gives you zero persistence on Pub/Sub.

statement: Neither is superior: for real time Redis is superior, for persistence Kafka is superior; there is no one answer, it is very contextual.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: In case of real time, yes, Redis is superior. In case of persistence, yes, Kafka is superior.

statement: A student suggested that in the Kafka (asynchronous persistence) approach a user could receive a message a day after it was sent, if the messaging-service workers pick it up from Kafka a day late.
detail: Teacher's correction: in that approach the message is sent as a real-time notification to users immediately; only storage is delayed - 'not delivered, stored'.
case_study: Slack real-time messaging design (the lecture's running case study).
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: Not delivered, stored. Delivered to immediately.

statement: With asynchronous persistence, if processing is delayed the source of truth does not have the message yet, so a user who refreshes the page will not see a message they already saw in real time.
case_study: Slack real-time messaging design (the lecture's running case study).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So if this does delay in processing, the source of truth does not have the data yet.

statement: Live streaming (e.g. Hotstar) is very different from real-time text communication and is out of scope here; a few bits will be touched in week six or seven.
detail: The teacher also recommended a streaming-related documentation he called very good (name unclear).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Hotstar live streaming is very different. We'll touch upon few bits and pieces of it in week seven, but not this part.

statement: There is no best way to build the system: the teacher laid out three types of persistence/messaging, different communication and privacy options - an entire buffet - and you build your own plate based on the guarantees you give your customers.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I have laid an entire buffet. It's for you to create your own plate, whatever works for you.

statement: A student working on a multi-level marketing hierarchy that is getting hard in a relational DB proposed a graph database; the teacher agreed: if it is painful and you need to find 3rd, 5th or 10th-level depth in the tree, a graph database makes more sense because joins and self-joins become a pain.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: In that case, graph database might make much more sense than relational, because then joins and queries and self joins become a pain

statement: Querying 10 levels deep means nine self-joins on a database, which is messy and something you typically don't want to do.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: nine self joins on a database is messy. Like you typically don't want to do that.

statement: A student argued message deletion must be synchronous with both flows (real-time and refresh) so a user doesn't see a deletion notification and then the message again after a refresh; the teacher questioned whether you really get a deletion notification at all.
case_study: Slack real-time messaging design (the lecture's running case study).
speaker: student (question)
verbatim: Do you really get deletion notification? No.

statement: WhatsApp does not store anything (messages are not kept on the server).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: WhatsApp does not store anything, FYI.

statement: WhatsApp-style deletion: send a message saying 'delete this message permanently' and delete it from the users' local storage on both sides.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Otherwise you can just add a message that I delete this message permanently and then just delete it from the user's local storage.

statement: Slack-style deletion: delete the message in the backend store and tell the user it is deleted; to communicate it in real time, also notify the users that it is now deleted.
case_study: Slack real-time messaging design (the lecture's running case study).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: if you're talking about Slack, you go over here, delete and tell the user that it's deleted.

statement: The architecture extends to any such question: depending on the guarantees, you just alter the approach within the same building blocks.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Depending on the guarantees, you just alter your approach.

statement: Even after doing the whole analysis, it took the teacher three and a half months with a three-engineer team to build a real-time text chat system; it takes time.
detail: Context: a student asked why WhatsApp took so long to add deletion if it is so easily extensible.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: it took me three and a half months, three engineer team to build it.

statement: Doing a feature like deletion at WhatsApp scale is humongous: hierarchy, deciding whether it is needed and how best to do it, product decisions and staggered rollout all take time from the product manager's idea to implementation.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: And plus doing it in WhatsApp scale is humongous.

statement: If the requirements are known and the system follows this architecture, supporting message deletion is a small change: about 100-200 lines, at most 200-300 lines of backend code (one event stored, one notification sent).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: the backend code changes would have been hardly 200 300 lines, not more than that, if they were with this architecture.

statement: Implement this yourself: work with WebSockets and mimic a 'message deleted' flow in the UI.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Like just work with WebSockets and try to do that, mimic that message deleted, see it in UI.

statement: Asked about message ordering and exactly-once semantics, the teacher challenged why exactly-once semantics is being added at all; nobody said it is required here.
case_study: Slack real-time messaging design (the lecture's running case study).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Why are we adding that exactly-once semantics?

statement: No one says messages must arrive strictly in order on screen: the front end can insert a message in the middle. Ordering matters where messages are processed one after another.
case_study: Slack real-time messaging design (the lecture's running case study).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Your front end insert the message in the middle. What's the problem?

statement: Ordering case 1: if user A sends message 1 then 2 and message 2 reaches user B first, render them in arrival order; on refresh the order gets fixed, because the order in which messages are stored in the database is the source of truth.
case_study: Slack real-time messaging design (the lecture's running case study).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you change the order, because the order in which it is stored in the database is the source of truth for you.

statement: Ordering case 2: keep the front-end (e.g. React) state ordered by timestamp; when an older message arrives late, insert it in the middle of the array instead of appending, accepting a brief flicker if that is okay for the user experience.
case_study: Slack real-time messaging design (the lecture's running case study).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So instead of appending it at the end of the array, you insert it in the middle.

statement: A student observed that on Microsoft Teams receivers sometimes get missing, duplicate or out-of-order messages that later get reshuffled into order.
speaker: student (question)
verbatim: Sometimes you'll get duplicate messages and sometimes you'll get out of order messages.

statement: Duplicates can be explained with this architecture: the system may broadcast to the receiver first and persist later, or it may retry on the WebSocket server when it thinks a message was not delivered although it actually was.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Even if they think that message is not delivered, but it was actually delivered.

statement: In this lecture's design the message is first stored, and only once storage is sure is the other user told the message exists.
case_study: Slack real-time messaging design (the lecture's running case study).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: then we tell the other user that this is there.

statement: Order gets fixed automatically either on page refresh (the source-of-truth API is called) or by a background job, e.g. every one minute call the HTTP backend for the last 50 messages, check they are all on the UI, and reorder if needed.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: every one minute you make a call to your back end, actual HTTP back end, to fetch the last 50 messages that you receive

statement: The message timestamp used for ordering is always the DB insertion time, according to the database's clock.
detail: Asked by a student which parameter decides the stored order.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It's always the DB insertion time, whatever it is, whatever is the clock on the DB is the time at which I'm inserting.

statement: A student proposed ordering messages by a timestamp sent from the client side.
detail: Teacher's correction: never send or rely on client timestamps when processing messages on the database - a user can just change their clock (e.g. to 1 January 1970); whatever time is on the database is the source of truth.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: Why do you want to send timestamps from the client? You should never do that when you're processing the message on the database.

statement: Messages like 'Hey', 'hi', 'hello' are never sent at exactly the same time from a client; there is always some time difference from typing and sending.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you can never send it at the exact same time.
flags: check: diarization seam - "they would never happen on the" may be the Teacher

statement: If network latency makes a later message arrive first, that is fine: whatever order the database received is the source of truth.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Whatever I received, whatever I received at my database, that's a source of truth for me.

statement: The overly complicated way to get true ordering is CRDTs for merge/conflict resolution and vector clocks on the client side, each client having its own vector clock persisted in the database.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: use CRDT to merge to conflict resolution. Use vector clocks on the client side.

statement: Vector clocks are not worth it here: maintaining them and doing merge conflicts on read slows down the whole system, and no one does that; don't re-architect for one edge case.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Having the complexity of maintaining vector clock, doing the merge conflicts when you read it slows down your entire system.

statement: Design realistic systems: theoretically you can find 100 loopholes, but practically there are few and it is okay to live with them; ask how likely the case is and whether you really need it, and implement only if yes.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Think on realistic terms. Do you really need that? If yes, then implement it.

statement: Vector clocks are the answer if you truly need it, but a globally consistent vector clock per client is a massive problem; look up its implementation to see how complicated it gets.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Massive problem. No one does that.

statement: The message store in this design is just sharded; replicas are optional, and the teacher saw no need for replication there.
detail: A student had assumed a master-slave replicated setup.
case_study: Slack real-time messaging design (the lecture's running case study).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Where is replication? There's just sharded. You can have replicas if you want, but typical sharded would work.

statement: To avoid losing a write when a DB node dies mid-write, important data is stored with standby nodes and a replication factor of three: each write goes to three data nodes, so if one goes down the others serve the data (as DynamoDB does internally).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You would have replication factor three-way persistent.

statement: After workers have processed messages from Kafka, you cannot recover a lost write by reading from Kafka again.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You cannot read from Kafka. You would already processed the messages.
flags: check: context of "You cannot read from Kafka" unclear

statement: A student suggested the workers themselves push each message to two or three different DB instances across regions for durability.
detail: Teacher's correction: workers doing that is worse; the replicated/distributed database's storage engine does it - a write comes to one data node, which replicates it to two others, so if one node goes down another serves the data.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: Your worker is not doing that, database is doing database. No, database storage engine is doing that.

statement: A replicated database never acknowledges (commits) a write until it has been written in three different places; a write lost before replication was simply never accepted.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Your DB would never say that I am done unless it is written in three different places.

statement: The worker holds the message until the DB commits it, retries otherwise, and if the worker goes down the message is reprocessed.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: so worker actually holds the state, holds the message until unless the DB commits it.
flags: check: "Correct. Correct." possibly Teacher back-channel - diarization

statement: When you write to DynamoDB, it is internally written to three different storage nodes, and only after all three complete does it report the write as complete.
detail: The teacher notes this goes deep into distributed database implementation.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: When you write to a DynamoDB, internally it gets written to three different storage nodes.

statement: Sharing a database between the workers and the API servers is perfectly fine; making workers call the API so the API writes to the DB adds an unnecessary network call and complication.
case_study: Slack real-time messaging design (the lecture's running case study).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: No, sharing a database is fine. Perfectly fine.

statement: The teacher dislikes the anti-pattern that every microservice needs its own database; he prioritizes performance and cost efficiency and is fine sharing a database.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I hate that anti-pattern where every microservice needs to have a separate database.

statement: Business and product come first, engineering second: do whatever keeps cost down and gets maximum performance, because the business is what keeps engineers employed.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Business and product comes first, engineering is all okay, right?

statement: The teacher's YouTube microservices playlist (17-18 videos) covers shared versus separate databases as a pattern, with advantages and disadvantages; two videos are on this topic.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: 17, 18 videos are there in that series. Two of them are basically around this topic
flags: check: possible ASR duplicate - "I have a video on it." x3

statement: On end-to-end encryption (pushing group members' public keys from the database), the teacher said he has no experience with public-key encryption; he knows the Signal protocol a bit, WhatsApp uses a variant of it, but he could not comment on what information it needs.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I know Signal protocol a bit. WhatsApp uses a variant of it, 100%, but I don't know what all information it needs

statement: A student proposed storing only private/public on a channel instead of a channel type, treating a DM as a private channel with two members.
detail: Teacher's correction: then you cannot differentiate a channel with two people from a DM, and they need to be rendered differently on the UI (the type is stored so the UI can render accordingly).
case_study: Slack real-time messaging design (the lecture's running case study).
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: How will you differentiate between a channel with two people and a DM?
flags: check: "Revisit your recording. Revisit." may be the Teacher speaking (diarization)

statement: A private channel created with two people can later get more members, but in a DM you cannot add more people; that is why the UI needs the channel type to render them differently.
case_study: Slack real-time messaging design (the lecture's running case study).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: But in DM, I cannot add more people to that.

statement: Private two-person channels, public two-person channels and two-person DMs can all exist, and a DM might be made private or public tomorrow; the explicit type keeps the schema extensible.
case_study: Slack real-time messaging design (the lecture's running case study).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: DM can also be made private or can also be made public tomorrow if they want to. Right. You just want to keep things extensible.

statement: The six-connection limit applies per host name (the full domain including sub-domains), so chat.google.com, Gmail and Meet each get their own six connections.
detail: The student also asked whether the limit is shared among tabs; the answer given addresses only sub-domains.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So it's at the domain level.

speaker: student (question)
verbatim: I have read that there is also a web transport specification coming up, right?

statement: A student proposed that, since WhatsApp stores data on the user's device while Slack stores it in the backend database, Slack should load old data via API calls rather than over WebSockets; the teacher agreed.
case_study: Slack real-time messaging design (the lecture's running case study).
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: the way or the communication channel to refresh the data should be API rather than doing it via

case_study: Slack real-time messaging design (the lecture's running case study).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you just see, oh my God, there are 200 unread messages.

statement: WhatsApp has to deliver messages to your device because that is where they are stored.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So WhatsApp has to get those messages delivered to you on your device, because it is stored as you

statement: All these systems are interconnected: with a few changes here and there you get a brand-new system; one pattern fits everywhere.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: This is one pattern fits everywhere.

statement: Closing: next week covers distributed systems and ID generators (pre-reads shared today); implement everything as a small hello world, especially Redis Pub/Sub - ten minutes of use shows how it pushes and gives no persistence.
